meta.dropDefinition: In the model menu, one drop equals the derived operational water of one short GPT-4o query (100 input tokens, 300 output tokens): Jegham et al. 2025 Table 4 mean energy passed through their equation (3). The glass is etched at 20 mL. Campus mode uses a different etching: a full glass is 4 million gallons per day.

figures.name: GPT-4o
figures.subtitle: ChatGPT-class · short prompt
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short query (100 input / 300 output tokens): on-site cooling plus off-site electricity. Scope 3 manufacturing water is excluded, matching Jegham et al.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham, Hamid, et al. How Hungry is AI? Benchmarking Energy, Water, and Carbon Footprint of LLM Inference
figures.notes: This row is the drop reference: one short GPT-4o query ≈ one drop. Energy is the Table 4 mean for the March 2025 GPT-4o snapshot, 0.421 ± 0.127 Wh, which already includes PUE. Water uses equation (3) with the paper's Microsoft Azure multipliers for this model class: PUE 1.12, on-site WUE 0.30 L/kWh, off-site WUE 3.142 L/kWh. The range propagates the reported energy standard deviation linearly. It is not a measured OpenAI disclosure.
figures.assumptions: E_kWh = Wh/1000. Water_L = (E_kWh / PUE) * WUE_site + E_kWh * WUE_source. Hardware class and batch size (8) are the paper's, not independent measurements.

figures.name: Claude 3.7 Sonnet
figures.subtitle: About two drops · short prompt
figures.boundary: Same short-prompt operational boundary as the GPT-4o row (on-site cooling + off-site electricity).
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4 and equation 3)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 0.836 ± 0.102 Wh. AWS multipliers from the paper's Table 1 for Anthropic models: PUE 1.14, on-site WUE 0.18 L/kWh, U.S. off-site WUE 3.142 L/kWh. About 1.9 times the GPT-4o short-query estimate, so the glass pours two drops. No per-query water figure for Claude Opus was found; Opus is not given this Sonnet number.
figures.assumptions: Same water equation as the GPT-4o row, with AWS rather than Azure multipliers.

figures.name: Claude 3.7 Sonnet
figures.subtitle: Extended thinking · short prompt
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short extended-thinking query. Higher because the paper's measured API energy is higher, not because a separate Opus disclosure exists.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4, Claude-3.7 Sonnet ET)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 3.490 ± 0.304 Wh for extended thinking, same AWS multipliers as Claude 3.7 Sonnet. About eight GPT-4o drops. This is the higher-use Claude mode in that paper. Anthropic has not published an Opus water-per-query figure in the sources reviewed.
figures.assumptions: Extended thinking is a different workload from a plain Sonnet reply. Do not read this as an Opus 4 measurement.

figures.name: GPT-4
figures.subtitle: Short prompt · A100-class estimate
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short query. The paper assigns GPT-4 to older A100-class nodes, which is why this short prompt is thirstier than GPT-4o.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4 and section 4.3.1)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 1.978 ± 0.419 Wh. Azure multipliers PUE 1.12, on-site WUE 0.30 L/kWh, off-site WUE 3.142 L/kWh. Long-prompt energy is blank in Table 4; only the short-prompt column is used. Hardware (DGX A100) is the authors' estimate, marked with an asterisk in their table.
figures.assumptions: A100 attribution is inferred by Jegham et al. from latency, not confirmed by OpenAI.

figures.name: Llama 3.3 70B
figures.subtitle: Short prompt · open model
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short query on the paper's AWS hosting assumption for Meta models.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4, LLaMA-3.3 70B)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 0.247 ± 0.032 Wh. AWS multipliers PUE 1.14, on-site WUE 0.18 L/kWh, off-site WUE 3.142 L/kWh. Under one GPT-4o drop. Meta has not published a per-query water figure for Llama; this is the paper's infrastructure model.
figures.assumptions: Host is taken as AWS, as in Jegham et al. Table 1, not a Meta disclosure of serving location.

figures.name: Llama 3.1 405B
figures.subtitle: Short prompt · largest Llama in the paper
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short query.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4, LLaMA-3.1-405B)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 1.991 ± 0.315 Wh with the same AWS multipliers as Llama 3.3 70B. About 4.6 GPT-4o drops.
figures.assumptions: Same equation and AWS multipliers as the other Meta rows in Jegham et al.

figures.name: OpenAI o3
figures.subtitle: Reasoning model · short prompt
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short o3 query. The wide range follows the wide energy standard deviation in Table 4.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4, o3)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 7.026 ± 3.663 Wh. Azure multipliers PUE 1.12, on-site WUE 0.30 L/kWh, off-site WUE 3.142 L/kWh. The mean sits above the 20 mL glass, so the faucet fills the glass and a little spills. Most of the water is off-site electricity, not the cooling tower.
figures.assumptions: Linear propagation of the energy standard deviation. The paper's o3 energy spread is large, so this range is wide on purpose.

figures.name: DeepSeek-R1
figures.subtitle: Short prompt · highest in this set
figures.boundary: Operational water for one short query using the paper's China data-center multipliers, which are much thirstier than the U.S. cloud rows.
figures.sourceTitle: Jegham et al., How Hungry is AI? (Table 4 and the water discussion of DeepSeek-R1)
figures.notes: Table 4 mean energy 23.815 ± 2.160 Wh. Multipliers from Table 1: PUE 1.27, on-site WUE 1.20 L/kWh, off-site WUE 6.016 L/kWh. The paper states DeepSeek-R1 consumes more than 150 mL per query; this derivation is 166 mL at the short-prompt mean, inside that description. The glass holds 20 mL and the rest runs to the drain. The authors attribute the size of this footprint to deployment infrastructure, not only to model architecture.
figures.assumptions: Off-site WUE is the paper's China grid factor, so this row is not comparable to a U.S. Azure deployment of the same model.

figures.name: Gemini Apps
figures.subtitle: Median text prompt · May 2025
figures.boundary: Google's comprehensive serving measurement: water consumed to cool machines and associated infrastructure for the median Gemini Apps text prompt. Not the same boundary as the short-prompt derivations above.
figures.sourceTitle: Elsworth et al., Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale
figures.notes: Table 2: 0.26 mL per prompt on the comprehensive approach and 0.12 mL on the narrower existing approach. The prose also describes a narrower method near 0.15 mL; the table values are what the glass uses for the range. Google says 0.26 mL is about five drops of 0.05 mL. On this simulator's scale one drop is a short GPT-4o query (1.44 mL), so Gemini is a small bead, not five of those drops. Fleet WUE in the paper is 1.15 L/kWh (ISO WUE category 2) for 2023 and 2024.
figures.assumptions: The range is the paper's two reported accounting boundaries, not a statistical confidence interval.

figures.name: ChatGPT
figures.subtitle: Average query · company claim
figures.boundary: Undisclosed. Altman did not say whether this is on-site cooling only, a narrow accelerator measurement, or a full operational footprint.
figures.sourceTitle: Sam Altman, The Gentle Singularity
figures.notes: Altman wrote that an average ChatGPT query uses about 0.34 Wh and about 0.000085 gallons of water, 'roughly one fifteenth of a teaspoon.' 0.000085 U.S. gallons = 0.322 mL. OpenAI published no methodology. Google's later paper flags the same gap. Do not line this up against the 17 mL or 519 mL academic figures as if the boundaries match.
figures.assumptions: Unit conversion uses 1 U.S. gallon = 3,785.411784 mL. No uncertainty range is stated by the source, so none is invented.

figures.name: GPT-3
figures.subtitle: ChatGPT-era medium response · U.S. average
figures.boundary: Operational water per medium-length request in Li et al. Table 1: on-site cooling plus off-site electricity. Embodied water is excluded. This is not a 2025 GPT-4o measurement.
figures.sourceTitle: Li, Yang, Islam, and Ren, Making AI Less “Thirsty”: Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
figures.notes: Table 1, U.S. average: 2.200 mL on-site, 14.704 mL off-site, 16.904 mL total, or 29.6 requests per 500 mL. Across locations in that table the total runs from 7.107 mL (Ireland) to 47.506 mL (Washington). The paper summarizes the same idea as a 500 mL bottle for roughly 10–50 medium-length responses (about 10–50 mL). Per-request server energy in the updated paper is about 0.004 kWh before location-specific PUE, WUE, and electricity water intensity. Training, reported separately, is not poured into this glass: U.S. training is 0.708 million liters on-site and 5.439 million liters total in the same table, and the abstract's often-quoted on-site training figure is 700,000 liters.
figures.assumptions: The glass uses the U.S. average point estimate. The range is the min and max location totals printed in Table 1, not a confidence interval. Locations marked as under construction in the paper are included in that min/max.

figures.name: Mistral Large 2
figures.subtitle: Le Chat · 400-token response
figures.boundary: Marginal inference impact of a 400-token Le Chat response, excluding the user's device. Mistral's lifecycle study also reports training separately.
figures.sourceTitle: Mistral AI, Our contribution to a global environmental standard for AI
figures.notes: Mistral, with Carbone 4 and ADEME, and a critical review by Resilio and Hubblo, reports 45 mL of water, 1.14 gCO2e, and 0.16 mg Sb eq for that response. Training through January 2025 is reported separately as 281,000 m³ of water and 20.4 ktCO2e and is not what the glass pours. The ADEME library record is dated July 2025 (posted 21 August 2025). No uncertainty band is published for the 45 mL figure.
figures.assumptions: A 400-token answer is a longer task than the 100/300-token short prompt used for the Jegham rows.

figures.name: GPT-4
figures.subtitle: 100-word email · 2024 estimate
figures.boundary: Water for GPT-4 to write one average 100-word email at an average U.S. data center, as calculated for The Washington Post with UC Riverside researchers. A different task and year from the short-prompt rows.
figures.sourceTitle: Pranshu Verma and Shelly Tan, A bottle of water per email, The Washington Post
figures.notes: The Post's 18 September 2024 story, reported with UC Riverside, says a GPT-4 100-word email uses 519 mL at an average American data center — the graphic's 'once' figure, consistent with their 'once weekly for a year ≈ 27 liters' (52 × 519 mL ≈ 27.0 L). The headline frames it as about a bottle of water per email. The live article page available during this research was truncated before the graphic; 519 mL is taken from the article text as captured from https://archive.ph/QD678 and checked against that weekly total. It is an estimate for a specific email task, not a measured OpenAI meter, and it is not comparable to Altman's 0.32 mL claim or Google's 0.26 mL Gemini figure without reading the boundary.
figures.assumptions: No uncertainty range was printed beside 519 mL in the sources used here, so the glass uses the reported point value and does not invent a band.

figures.name: Grok
figures.subtitle: No published per-query figure
figures.boundary: Not applicable. A per-query number is not published.
figures.sourceTitle: No per-query water disclosure found for Grok
figures.notes: xAI has not published a water-per-query figure for Grok, and Jegham et al. 2025 does not include Grok. Inventing one from a neighbor model's energy would be a new estimate, not a cited one, so the glass pours out and stays empty. Campus water for Colossus and Colossus 2 is in the Data Centers menu. The linked story is about Memphis water supply, not a query.
figures.assumptions: Absence of a figure is treated as a gap, not as zero water.

figures.name: Colossus & Colossus 2
figures.subtitle: xAI Memphis · both sites
figures.boundary: Requested municipal drinking-water cap for the original Colossus data center and the second site together. Not a meter reading, and not a split that isolates Colossus 2.
figures.sourceTitle: Ariel Wittenberg and Miranda Willson, Musk promised his data center would reuse water. That's now stalled. E&E News by POLITICO
figures.notes: E&E News, 4 May 2026: 'The company has requested to use up to 3.7 million gallons of water a day, both at its original data center and second site a few miles away that will not draw from the planned reuse facility, MLGW said.' Colossus 2 is the Tulane Road site. No separately published measured daily volume for Colossus 2 alone was found, so this card is the combined request. The greywater plant meant to replace aquifer withdrawals was paused in April 2026.
figures.assumptions: 3.7 million is an upper request stated by the utility via E&E, not average consumption.

figures.name: Council Bluffs, Iowa
figures.subtitle: Google · 2023 consumption
figures.boundary: Annual water consumption (withdrawal minus discharge) at the Council Bluffs campus, divided by 365. On-site data-center water, not electricity-generation water.
figures.sourceTitle: Google 2024 Environmental Report, Water use by data center location 2023
figures.notes: Potable water, Council Bluffs, IA: withdrawal 1,334.9 million gallons, discharge 354.8 million gallons, consumption 980.1 million gallons. Daily average consumption = 980,100,000 / 365 = 2,685,205 gal/day. Withdrawal averages 3,657,260 gal/day and is not what the glass pours. Google's global data centers consumed 6.1 billion gallons in 2023. Consumption is evaporated or otherwise not returned, per Google's definition in that report.
figures.assumptions: A flat 365-day year. 2023 was not a leap year. The report does not publish a daily time series, so the glass shows the annual average, not a summer peak.

figures.name: Mayes County, Oklahoma
figures.subtitle: Google · 2023 consumption
figures.boundary: Annual campus consumption divided by 365. On-site only.
figures.sourceTitle: Google 2024 Environmental Report, Water use by data center location 2023
figures.notes: Mayes County, OK, potable water: withdrawal 1,037.1 million gallons, discharge 222.0 million gallons, consumption 815.1 million gallons. Daily average consumption = 815,100,000 / 365 = 2,233,151 gal/day.
figures.assumptions: Annual total divided by 365. Not a measured daily peak.

figures.name: Berkeley County, South Carolina
figures.subtitle: Google · 2023 consumption
figures.boundary: Annual campus consumption divided by 365. On-site only.
figures.sourceTitle: Google 2024 Environmental Report, Water use by data center location 2023
figures.notes: Berkeley County, SC, potable water: withdrawal 847.2 million gallons, discharge 83.8 million gallons, consumption 763.4 million gallons. Daily average consumption = 763,400,000 / 365 = 2,091,507 gal/day.
figures.assumptions: Annual total divided by 365.

figures.name: Meta data centers
figures.subtitle: Global fleet · 2023 consumption
figures.boundary: Fleet-wide data-center water consumption, not one campus. Offices are excluded (140 ML in the same table).
figures.sourceTitle: Meta 2024 Sustainability Report, data index, water consumption
figures.notes: Data centers total water consumption in 2023: 2,938 megaliters. 2,938 ML = 2.938 billion liters = 776,137,336 U.S. gallons, using 3.785411784 L/gal. Daily average = 776,137,336 / 365 = 2,126,404 gal/day. Meta's 2023 annual data-center WUE was 0.18 L/kWh. This card is the whole fleet; Fort Worth and Prineville below are withdrawals at single sites.
figures.assumptions: Megaliters in the report are treated as 1 ML = 1,000 m³. Year length 365.

figures.name: Colossus
figures.subtitle: xAI · Paul R. Lowry Road
figures.boundary: Contracted peak municipal supply for data-center cooling at the first Memphis site. Not metered average consumption, and not Colossus 2.
figures.sourceTitle: The Commercial Appeal and Memphis Light, Gas and Water public descriptions of the xAI water agreement
figures.notes: The Commercial Appeal (5 June 2025), citing the MLGW agreement: peak monthly demand of 39,000,062 gallons, 'or roughly 1.3 million gallons daily,' for data-center cooling. The Tennessean (12 March 2025) reports the same June 10 contract figure and the same daily description; ignore the extra word 'million' in one sentence of that story — the gallon count is 39,000,062. MLGW's 2024 quick-facts sheet says 'up to 1 MGD' from an existing main (https://www.mlgw.com/images/content/files/pdf/2024xAI%20and%20MLGW%20Quick%20Facts%201.pdf). A 9 July 2024 city briefing says the same ~1 MGD addition (https://memphistn.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/xAI-water-and-electric-7-9-24-final.pdf). The Commercial Appeal on 6 May 2025 describes the contracts as peak demand up to 1.4 million gallons a day (https://www.commercialappeal.com/story/news/local/2025/05/06/xai-seeks-1-gigawatt-of-power-memphis-site/83453645007/). The glass uses 1.3 million gal/day and shows 1.0–1.4 million as the spread of those public descriptions.
figures.assumptions: 1.3 million gal/day is the newspapers' daily reading of a peak monthly contract quantity, not 39,000,062 / 30.4 computed independently as a new estimate. The range is disagreement among public descriptions, not a confidence interval.

figures.name: The Dalles, Oregon
figures.subtitle: Google · 2023 consumption
figures.boundary: Google's 2023 on-site consumption for The Dalles, annual total divided by 365. A city meter for 2024 is a different metric and is not poured.
figures.sourceTitle: Google 2024 Environmental Report, Water use by data center location 2023
figures.notes: The Dalles, OR, potable water: withdrawal 383.7 million gallons, discharge 81.3 million gallons, consumption 302.4 million gallons. Daily average consumption = 302,400,000 / 365 = 828,493 gal/day. Separately, OPB (23 January 2026), citing city records, says Google used 434.4 million gallons in 2024 (about 1.19 million gallons a day). That city figure is municipal delivery for a later year, so it is cited here and not mixed into the poured consumption number. https://www.opb.org/article/2026/01/23/the-dalles-mayor-data-center-google/
figures.assumptions: Annual consumption divided by 365.

figures.name: Fort Worth, Texas
figures.subtitle: Meta · 2023 withdrawal
figures.boundary: Site withdrawal, not consumption. Meta publishes consumption for the fleet, not for this campus.
figures.sourceTitle: Meta 2024 Sustainability Report, water withdrawal by facility
figures.notes: Fort Worth withdrawal in 2023: 404 megaliters, the largest U.S. campus in that facility table. 404 ML = 106,725,488 U.S. gallons; daily average = 292,399 gal/day. Clonee, Ireland was higher (659 ML) but is not an AI-specific U.S. hyperscale card. Do not compare this withdrawal directly with a Google consumption card without the badge.
figures.assumptions: 1 ML = 1,000,000 L; 1 U.S. gallon = 3.785411784 L; year length 365.

figures.name: West Des Moines, Iowa
figures.subtitle: Microsoft campus · utility meter
figures.boundary: Water the city utility attributes to Microsoft's West Des Moines data centers. Metered supply, not evaporative consumption, and not an AI-only load.
figures.sourceTitle: West Des Moines Water Works, Data Centers and Water Usage
figures.notes: WDMWW table: Microsoft data center water use was 68.58 million gallons in 2024 (2.6% of water pumped) and 62.34 million gallons in 2025 (2.4%). 2024 is a leap year, so the poured daily average is 68,580,000 / 366 = 187,377 gal/day. The low end of the range is the 2025 total divided by 365 (170,795 gal/day). The page was read on 24 September 2026. Microsoft's own FY2023 sustainability fact sheet reports company-wide water consumption of 7,844 megaliters and does not break out this campus, so the utility meter is used instead.
figures.assumptions: 2024 divided by 366; 2025 divided by 365. The utility page presents 2025 as a full year in the same table as prior years.

figures.name: Prineville, Oregon
figures.subtitle: Meta · 2023 withdrawal
figures.boundary: Site withdrawal. Prineville is shown because it is a long-running Meta campus with a much smaller withdrawal than the Google evaporative campuses.
figures.sourceTitle: Meta 2024 Sustainability Report, water withdrawal by facility
figures.notes: Prineville withdrawal in 2023: 180 megaliters = 47,550,933 U.S. gallons; daily average = 130,277 gal/day. Withdrawal at this site has fallen from 445 ML in 2020 in the same table. Consumption for the site is not separately published.
figures.assumptions: Same liter-to-gallon conversion and 365-day year as the other Meta rows.

contextOnly.name: GPT-3 training, U.S. data centers
contextOnly.sourceTitle: Li et al., Making AI Less “Thirsty,” Table 1
contextOnly.notes: Not poured. Table 1 U.S. average training water is 0.708 million liters on-site and 5.439 million liters total. The abstract also states 700,000 liters of scope-1 on-site freshwater. Training is a one-time (or occasional) total, not a daily campus meter and not a per-query figure.

contextOnly.name: Colossus water recycle plant, design allocation to xAI
contextOnly.sourceTitle: The Tennessean, citing the February 2025 TDEC application for the Colossus Water Recycle Plant
contextOnly.notes: Not poured, and not operating. The Tennessean (12 March 2025) says the application describes about 5 million gallons daily to xAI, about 7 million to TVA, and a peak plant demand around 13.5 million gallons daily. E&E News (4 May 2026) reports construction paused in April 2026. A design allocation is not current use.

contextOnly.name: Amazon / AWS campuses
contextOnly.sourceTitle: No site-level Amazon water total is included
contextOnly.notes: Amazon's sustainability reporting has not publicly itemized data-center water the way Google's location table does. No Amazon campus is poured, rather than substituting a secondary estimate.
